title: Scalar characters on field generators and finite automorphism order
statement:
Let $E/F$ be a field extension [def-weil-field], [def-pc-field-extension], let $r\geq0$, and let $b_1,\ldots,b_r\in E^\times$ generate $E$ as a field over $F$: the smallest subfield containing the image of $F$ and all $b_j$ is $E$. Let $U\subseteq F^\times$ be finite, contain $1$, and be closed under multiplication and inversion, endowed with those operations. Put $G=\operatorname{Aut}_F(E)$, the group of field automorphisms fixing $F$, with composition as multiplication. Suppose that for every $\sigma\in G$ and every $j$ there exists $u\in U$ such that $\sigma(b_j)=u b_j$ (scalars are read through $F\hookrightarrow E$). Then there is a unique homomorphism of groups
$$\chi:G\longrightarrow U^r$$
satisfying $\sigma(b_j)=\chi(\sigma)_j b_j$ for all $\sigma,j$. It is injective. The group $G$ is finite and
$$|G|\mid |U|^r.$$
Here $U^r$ is the group of $r$-tuples with coordinatewise multiplication, and cardinalities are finite nonnegative integers. No algebraicity, normality or separability hypothesis on $E/F$ is imposed. The empty list is allowed: then the generating hypothesis says $E=F$ and $G$ and $U^0$ are trivial.

proof.text: Construct the character and prove its uniqueness. Identify $F$ with its image in $E$ using [def-pc-field-extension]. Since $U$ contains $1$ and is closed under multiplication and inverses, the field laws [def-weil-field] restrict to a commutative group on $U$; coordinatewise these laws give the group $U^r$. For each $\sigma,j$ the hypothesized scalar $u\in U$ is unique: $ub_j=vb_j$ implies $u=v$, by multiplying by $b_j^{-1}$ in the field [def-weil-field] and using the injectivity of $F\to E$. Define $\chi(\sigma)_j$ to be this unique scalar. Identity has scalar $1$. For composition, write $u=\chi(\sigma)_j$ and $v=\chi(\tau)_j$. Since $v\in F$, $\sigma$ fixes $v$, so $(\sigma\tau)(b_j)=\sigma(vb_j)=v\sigma(b_j)=vu b_j=uv b_j$. Closure of $U$ under multiplication and uniqueness of the scalar give $\chi(\sigma\tau)_j=\chi(\sigma)_j\chi(\tau)_j$. Thus $\chi$ is a group homomorphism for coordinatewise multiplication. Any other map with the stated coordinate formula equals $\chi$ at every $\sigma,j$, again by cancellation; in particular it is the unique such homomorphism.

source.place: Tag 09I6 (section-Kummer), opening paragraph: scalar character and its subgroup-order argument, expanded for a finite generating family.

proof.text: Prove injectivity directly. If $\chi(\sigma)=\chi(\tau)$, then $\sigma(b_j)=\tau(b_j)$ for every $j$. The equalizer $T=\{x\in E:\sigma(x)=\tau(x)\}$ contains $F$ and all $b_j$ and is a subfield: it contains $0,1$, and preservation of addition, negatives, multiplication and inverses by the two field automorphisms gives closure under those operations. The smallest-subfield generating hypothesis therefore gives $E\subseteq T$. Hence $\sigma(x)=\tau(x)$ for every $x\in E$, which says $\sigma=\tau$. This proves injectivity without an algebraicity hypothesis.

proof.text: The group $U^r$ is finite and has cardinality $|U|^r$: for $r=0$ there is one empty tuple, and adjoining one coordinate bijects the next tuple set with $U^r\times U$, multiplying its cardinality by $|U|$. Apply [lem-sfb-injective-hom-finite-group-order] with $A=G$, $B=U^r$, $f=\chi$ and the injectivity just proved. Its two conclusions give that $G$ is finite and $|G|\mid |U^r|=|U|^r$. If $r=0$, the generating hypothesis identifies $E$ with the image of $F$, so every $F$-automorphism is the identity, as asserted; the same conclusion follows from the injection into the singleton empty-tuple group.
